title: Self-Confidence Is Shaped by the People Whose Validation and Respect We Seek
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article distinguishes between people who anchor their self-worth externally, seeking validation from wide, often unknown audiences on social media, and those who anchor it internally, relying on feedback from a small circle of trusted people whose judgment they respect. It links a strong external anchor to lower well-being, higher anxiety, emotional volatility, and overreaction to criticism, since self-esteem becomes contingent on forces the person can't control. The piece offers practical guidance for leaders and parents who notice a team or family member's confidence swinging widely: redirect them toward the opinions of people who actually know their work well, rather than the noise of strangers.
points: People anchor their self-worth either externally (wide, often unknown audiences) or internally (a small circle of trusted judges).
Externally anchored people prioritize scale and reach over relevance, finding validation from strangers meaningful regardless of context.
A strong external anchor correlates with lower well-being, higher anxiety, more mood swings, and overreaction to criticism.
If someone's confidence swings widely, redirecting them toward trusted, informed judges rather than strangers can help stabilize it.
quotes: Some people anchor their self-worth and self-identity externally rather than internally.
The source of favorable views and social validation matters less than the speed and quantity of the attention they crave.
people with a strong external anchor experience lower well-being, higher anxiety, more mood swings, less intrinsic motivation, and more emotional volatility.
when a person’s sense of self-worth becomes too contingent on forces they don’t influence or control, their self-esteem and self-confidence can fluctuate wildly.
External validation from strangers doesn’t create lower self-confidence. It feeds it.
